## Why tiered triage

In a `bilatr` panel fit, dyads vary enormously in how much data they
contribute: some have hundreds of observed periods, others just a
handful. A sparse dyad's own latent trajectory (`theta`) is *expected*
to have a wide, poorly-identified posterior -- that's not a bug, it's
what little data looks like. Reading `fit$summary()` or
`fit$diagnostic_summary()` directly makes it easy to either drown in
that expected noise, or (worse) miss a real problem in a global/shared
parameter because it's buried among thousands of noisy per-dyad-period
rows.

[diagnose_convergence()] addresses this by classifying every monitored
quantity into one of three tiers before applying Rhat/ESS thresholds:

* **Tier 1 -- global/shared parameters** (`alpha`, `mu_intercept`,
  `sigma_theta0`, `mu_log_phi`, `sigma_log_phi`, `mu_log_noise`,
  `sigma_log_noise`, and `lp__`; `gamma`/`sigma_gamma` too, for the
  experimental `stable_gamma` variant). These affect the whole model, so
  any issue here is always reported in full, never summarized away.
* **Tier 2 -- per-dyad hierarchical parameters** (`phi`, `process_noise`,
  `theta0`, and their non-centered/raw counterparts). These are screened
  against how much data (`n_dt`) each dyad has, flagging dyads whose
  diagnostics are worse than a smooth degradation-with-sparsity trend
  would predict -- i.e. genuine outliers, not just the sparsest dyads.
* **Tier 3 -- per-dyad-period latent states** (`theta`, `theta_raw`).
  These are the noisiest by design, so they're reported only as
  per-dyad aggregate statistics (e.g. minimum ESS along a dyad's path),
  never flooding the console with one row per dyad-period.

## A panel with very uneven sparsity

We simulate a small panel where dyad activity spans two orders of
magnitude, to make the tiering concrete:


``` r
library(bilatr)
library(dplyr)

set.seed(42)
countries <- c("USA", "CHN", "RUS", "IRN", "PRK", "ISR")
dyad_pairs <- expand.grid(a1 = countries, a2 = countries, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) %>%
  filter(a1 != a2) %>%
  slice(1:8)

# very uneven event counts per dyad: some dyads get a handful of events,
# others hundreds.
n_events_per_dyad <- c(400, 350, 300, 250, 15, 10, 8, 5)
events <- purrr::map2_dfr(seq_len(nrow(dyad_pairs)), n_events_per_dyad, function(i, n) {
  dates <- format(
    sample(seq(as.Date("2015-01-01"), as.Date("2019-12-31"), by = "day"), n, replace = TRUE),
    "%Y%m%d"
  )
  tibble::tibble(
    Actor1CountryCode = dyad_pairs$a1[i],
    Actor2CountryCode = dyad_pairs$a2[i],
    SQLDATE = as.integer(dates),
    EventCode = sample(cameo_lookup$CAMEOEVENTCODE, n, replace = TRUE)
  )
})
events <- recode_cameo(events, code_col = "EventCode")
#> recode_cameo(): 13 row(s) matched a bare top-level CAMEO root code with no ModifiedRootCode (its sub-codes span several classes).

agg <- aggregate_events(
  events,
  grouping_var = "PentaClass",
  resolution = "yearly",
  start = "2015-01-01",
  end = "2019-12-31"
)
```


``` r
fit <- fit_panel(
  agg,
  reference_category = "1", # verbal cooperation
  min_n_events = 1,
  chunk_size = 4,
  chains = 2,
  parallel_chains = 2,
  threads_per_chain = 2,
  iter_warmup = 300,
  iter_sampling = 300,
  seed = 1,
  refresh = 0
)
```

As in the other vignettes, this run is deliberately short (and the event
data purely random, with no real signal for the model to recover); the
vignette was computed ahead of time, with CmdStan, and is kept quick to
re-run. That means it's a poor fit in an absolute
sense -- don't be surprised to see Tier 1 flags below that a longer,
real run wouldn't show. That's still a useful illustration: on a real
fit, any Tier 1 flag is exactly the kind of thing this tool is meant to
surface loudly rather than let it get lost among per-dyad noise.

## Running the triage

Tiers 2 and 3 judge each dyad against `n_dt`, its total number of
events. By default `diagnose_convergence()` computes it from the Stan
data that [fit_panel()] attached to the fit, and it also knows from the
fit which model was used:


``` r
diag <- diagnose_convergence(fit)
diag
#> <bilatr_diagnostics>
#> 
#> == Tier 1: global/shared parameters (16/16 flagged) ==

#>  4 mu_intercept[3]  2.01     3.02     4.36 TRUE
```

You can also pass your own `n_dt`, keyed by `dyad_id` (the dyad index
used inside the Stan model) or by dyad name. This is the same as the
default:


``` r
stan_data <- attr(fit, "stan_data")
n_dt <- tibble::tibble(
  dyad_id = seq_len(stan_data$D),
  n_dt = apply(stan_data$Y, 1, sum)
)
identical(diagnose_convergence(fit, n_dt = n_dt), diag)
#> [1] TRUE
```

The printed report separates concerns by tier: Tier 1 issues (if any)
are always shown in full; Tier 2 shows a compact per-dyad table sorted
so any dyad flagged as "worse than expected for its `n_dt`" appears
first; Tier 3 collapses to one-line aggregate statistics.

## Working with the pieces directly

`diag` is a plain list (class `bilatr_diagnostics`) with `tier1`,
`tier2`, `tier3`, `tier3_other` and `summary` elements (and `gamma`, for
a `stable_gamma` fit), so you can filter or join further as needed:


``` r
# any global/shared parameter that failed to converge:
dplyr::filter(diag$tier1, flagged)
#> # A tibble: 16 × 5
#>    variable         rhat ess_bulk ess_tail flagged
#>    <chr>           <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>
```

## Computing only some tiers

`tiers` (default `1:3`) restricts which tier(s) are computed at all --
useful since Tier 3 typically dwarfs the other two in the number of
monitored quantities (one per dyad-period), so computing Rhat/ESS for
it is the most expensive part of a call. A quick check of just the
global/shared parameters, which has no per-dyad structure and so does
not use `n_dt`, looks like:


``` r
diagnose_convergence(fit, tiers = 1)
#> <bilatr_diagnostics>
#> 
#> == Tier 1: global/shared parameters (16/16 flagged) ==
#> # A tibble: 16 × 5
#>    variable         rhat ess_bulk ess_tail flagged
#>    <chr>           <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>  
#>  1 lp__             1.97     2.81    NA    TRUE   
#>  2 mu_intercept[1]  2.01     3.74   162.   TRUE   
#>  3 mu_intercept[2]  1.64    28.7    111.   TRUE   
#>  4 mu_intercept[3]  2.01     3.02     4.36 TRUE   
#>  5 mu_intercept[4]  2.03     5.47   151.   TRUE   
#>  6 mu_intercept[5]  1.68   142.      92.4  TRUE   
#>  7 sigma_theta0     2.18     2.65    NA    TRUE   
#>  8 mu_log_noise     1.78    23.2    274.   TRUE   
#>  9 sigma_log_noise  1.77    33.7     85.5  TRUE   
#> 10 mu_log_phi       1.98     2.80    NA    TRUE   
#> 11 sigma_log_phi    1.92     2.90     4.20 TRUE   
#> 12 alpha[1]         1.66    13.4    146.   TRUE   
#> 13 alpha[2]         1.80     5.21     7.64 TRUE   
#> 14 alpha[3]         2.01    10.4     57.6  TRUE   
#> 15 alpha[4]         1.94     4.19   147.   TRUE   
#> 16 alpha[5]         1.88     5.71   137.   TRUE
```

`diag$tier2`/`diag$tier3` are `NULL` (not empty tibbles) for any tier
left out of `tiers`, so `is.null(diag$tier3)` distinguishes "not
computed" from "computed, nothing to report".

## Tuning thresholds

`rhat_threshold` (default `1.01`) and `ess_threshold` (default `400`,
applied to both `ess_bulk` and `ess_tail`) follow Vehtari et al. (2021)
and can be tightened or loosened:


``` r
diagnose_convergence(fit, rhat_threshold = 1.05, ess_threshold = 100)
```

## From CmdStan CSV files

On a cluster, or for any large fit, you will usually diagnose the
CmdStan CSV files rather than a fit object held in memory. Pass the file
paths: `diagnose_convergence()` finds the `*_stan_data.rds` file that
[fit_panel()] wrote next to them (with `output_dir`), which gives it
`n_dt` and the model, and reads Tier 3 in chunks whose size it derives
from `max_memory_mb`. The two levers for a large fit are:

* `max_memory_mb`: the memory budget per chunk. Fewer, larger chunks
  are faster, so use the largest budget your job can afford.
* `n_cores`: the number of processes that compute R-hat and ESS for
  each chunk. More cores are faster but use more memory, out of the same
  budget, so a large `n_cores` on a tight budget can mean more chunks.

The pre-flight message says how many chunks were chosen and the
estimated peak memory; [`vignette("tuning")`](tuning.html) has more on these settings.

This section runs when the vignette is built, without CmdStan, on the
small example fit that ships with bilatr ([bilatr_example_fit()]: 6
dyads, 2 chains of 60 draws, far too short to converge):

```{r}
library(bilatr)
csv_files <- bilatr_example_fit()
basename(csv_files)
diag_csv <- diagnose_convergence(csv_files, max_memory_mb = 2048)
diag_csv$summary[c("n_tier1_flagged", "n_tier1_total")]
diag_csv$tier3_other
```

## On the "worse than expected" flag

The Tier 2/3 outlier flag is deliberately simple: dyads are grouped
into `n_dt` quantile brackets, and a dyad is flagged when its ESS falls
more than 1.5 times the interquartile range below its own bracket's
median (the standard Tukey outlier rule). This means a very sparse
dyad with a wide, low-ESS posterior is *not* flagged as long as its
peers at similar sparsity look about the same -- only a dyad that
stands out *relative to equally-sparse peers* is surfaced, which is
the actual failure mode worth investigating (e.g. a data or
identification issue specific to that dyad, rather than sparsity
alone).
